item.title: Huang resigns from Nvidia as Google ships Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 / $7.50
item.description: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's chief executive and director with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, Harvey Jones is the company's first chair, and shares fell as much as 14% before recovering. Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen, a $1.50 / $7.50 agent model priced flat across a 1M context that retires the Flash name. Thinking Machines published Inkling 2 Small's 394 GB of weights under Apache 2.0. Four nonprofits sued five frontier labs in San Francisco to halt advanced model development, OpenAI backed four chip-export bills, and Arctic Wolf documented attackers running an open-source AI pentest platform against AWS accounts. Doximity found 63% of US physicians now use AI for clinical decisions, J.P. Morgan forecast up to 400,000 US humanoids a year by 2030, SpaceX's two data-centre proposals now total $74 billion, and a Microsoft 365 outage took Copilot and the AI connectors that depend on it offline for most of a day.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, November 17, with Kress presenting alone for the first time, one day before Anthropic prices its IPO with a $10 billion Nvidia commitment inside it. If you own, buy from or build on Nvidia, that call is the one event this month to clear your calendar for.

Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia with immediate effect; CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO and shares fell as much as 14%

Nvidia's Form 8-K says Huang resigned as president, CEO and director on November 12 after 33 years, gives no reason, and names long-time director Harvey Jones as the company's first chair. The resignation followed days of reporting on Huang's personal relationships, including one with a senior executive and alleged contact with a former Megaspeed executive accused of working for Chinese intelligence; Huang admitted infidelity, and the board says its independent investigation has found no reason to believe national security was compromised. Shares fell more than 14% intraday on Thursday before paring losses. Third-quarter results stay scheduled for November 17.

  • Finance: Earnings on November 17 are now the first call with an interim CEO, one day before Anthropic prices an IPO that includes a $10 billion Nvidia commitment. Guidance tone and that commitment are the two things to listen for.
  • Executives: The 8-K promises no interruption to the roadmap or customer commitments. Get your allocation confirmation in writing this week while that promise is fresh.
  • Security: Lawmakers are examining the national-security side of the reports; Semafor reports a 'high probability' of tighter export controls. If you rent GPUs overseas, the Remote Access Security Act is the bill to read.
  • ML engineers: Nothing changes in CUDA or the Blackwell/Rubin cadence this quarter. What could change is Nvidia's appetite for the $12.9 billion Hugging Face deal and its open-source posture; Hugging Face's CEO said Thursday he will keep fighting for it.
  • Beginners: The co-founder who ran the world's most valuable chip company for 33 years stepped down after a scandal. The finance chief is running it while the board looks for a replacement.

Source: Nvidia Form 8-K · Al Jazeera

Google releases Gemini 4 Hydrogen at $1.50 / $7.50, flat across 1M tokens, and retires the Flash brand

Google's new fast model for agents is priced at $1.50 per million input and $7.50 per million output tokens with no long-context surcharge and no promotional window, and is available in the Gemini API, AI Studio, Antigravity, Gemini Enterprise, Search and the Gemini app. Google reports it finishes tasks 2.5x faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, scores 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 against Flash's 18.2%, and edges Argon on the Artificial Analysis index at 51 versus 50. It adds a fourth 'xhigh' thinking level and is positioned as the worker model under Carbon in Google's Orchestrator.

  • Developers: Flat pricing across the full 1M window is the feature; a 600K-token agent run costs the same per token as a short one. Re-run your Flash evals on Hydrogen at thinking level high.
  • Finance: Hydrogen is double Flash's promotional rate but equal to Flash's post-promo price from January 1. From that date the only cost argument is Google's claim of 12–23% fewer tokens per task.
  • ML engineers: Google reports a 2.3x gain on Gray Swan's indirect prompt-injection benchmark and 12x fewer misaligned actions in tool-use evals. Internal numbers; ask for the methodology.
  • Executives: Google now sells a three-model line: Hydrogen executes, Carbon and Argon reason. Expect vendor proposals to split workloads that way, and price them that way.

Source: Google blog

Four nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX in San Francisco to halt frontier AI development

Public Citizen, the Heat Initiative, the Irreplaceable Education Fund and others filed on November 12 under California's unfair-business-practices and public-nuisance laws, seeking an order barring further development of models such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The complaint cites incidents in which models allegedly escaped test environments and quotes the labs' own leaders on civilisational risk. It follows Florida's pending motion to stop OpenAI training new models without oversight and an eight-state suit filed in October. Meta declined to comment; the others had not responded.

  • Executives: Injunctions against an industry's R&D are rare; discovery is the real cost. If a vendor's model were enjoined even briefly, does your contract let you substitute?
  • Finance: Filed six days before Anthropic prices its IPO in the same city. It will be in the risk factors and in every analyst question about regulatory overhang.
  • ML engineers: Your sandbox-escape reports and system cards are now potential exhibits. Write them as if a plaintiff will read them, because one will.
  • Beginners: Advocacy groups are asking a judge to stop the biggest AI companies from building more powerful models, using the companies' own warnings about danger as evidence.

Source: The Daily Record (Reuters)

Attackers ran AntiFox, an open-source AI pentest platform, from Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets: hundreds of API calls in 30 minutes

Arctic Wolf documented two intrusions in which self-hosted AntiFox agents, forked from the ARTEX framework, planted an ASPX webshell on an IIS server, read connection strings and config files, then cycled through AWS identities with hundreds of API requests in about half an hour; most were denied, some returned production secrets. A second case used a valid identity to read, copy and delete S3 objects. Amazon says its services operated as designed and the credentials came from compromised customer applications.

  • Security: Write the rule today: one principal, a burst of AccessDenied calls, a few successes, within minutes, correlated with new ASPX files. That is an agent enumerating permissions.
  • Developers: Both cases began with long-lived keys in application files. Move them to roles, require IMDSv2, and let GuardDuty see the burst.
  • Executives: The attack tooling is free and forkable. The cost of an automated intrusion campaign against your cloud is now a VM and an API key.
  • Beginners: Hackers used a free AI hacking toolkit to break into websites, find the passwords those sites used for Amazon's cloud, and steal data with them.

Source: BleepingComputer · Arctic Wolf

Thinking Machines publishes Inkling 2 Small's weights: 394 GB, Apache 2.0, 500 GB of VRAM to run, no stable serving stack yet

The 594B-parameter, 17B-active mixture-of-experts model landed on Hugging Face on November 12, three days after its hosted-only launch on Tinker, in Nvidia's NVFP4 format with an MXFP8 variant at 623 GB. The card asks for at least 500 GB of aggregate VRAM (2x B300 or 4x H200). As of Thursday SGLang and vLLM support it only in development builds, and the promised external red-team results were not published with the drop.

  • ML engineers: NVFP4-native weights target Blackwell; expert parallelism must equal tensor parallelism. Wait for a validated H200 or AMD path unless you have B300s.
  • Developers: Hosted is $0.30 / $1.00 on Tinker. Self-hosting on four H200s only wins at sustained high utilisation.
  • Executives: Apache 2.0 with a patent grant on a 594B model is as permissive as licences get. The legal review is short; the GPU bill is the decision.
  • Finance: Thinking Machines is giving away the model and selling the fine-tuning platform. That is the business model to price when its next round comes.

Source: OrcaRouter · AlphaSignal

Doximity: 63% of US physicians use AI for clinical decision support, up from 37% a year ago, and three in four hit a factual error

Doximity's survey of 3,379 physicians across 20 specialties, fielded in September and published November 12, finds more than half use AI daily and a further third weekly. Use has moved from documentation to judgment: 63% use it for clinical decision support (37% in 2025) and 70% for literature review. 81% say it taught them something; three in four encountered at least one factual inaccuracy in the past year; 61% worry trainees will not build their own skills.

  • Executives: Clinicians are already using AI for decisions, mostly on tools you do not manage. Offer a sanctioned, logged one before trying to block the rest.
  • Security: Daily clinical use on consumer chatbots means PHI in prompts. A sanctioned tool with logging is the control that works.
  • ML engineers: Three in four doctors found an error and most kept using the tool. Your clinical evals should report error rate on real queries, because buyers will ask.
  • Beginners: Doctors increasingly ask AI for second opinions on diagnoses. Most say it has taught them something, and most say it has also been wrong, so they check.

Source: Healthcare Dive

J.P. Morgan forecasts 300,000–400,000 US humanoid robots a year by 2030 and names hands, actuators, the brain and capacity as the bottlenecks

In a note reported by Reuters on Thursday, J.P. Morgan projects US humanoid output of 300,000 to 400,000 units by 2030 and about 1.5 million by 2035, with most makers other than Tesla targeting 10,000 to 30,000 units a year. It sizes the actuator, motor and vision component market at nearly $30 billion by 2035, estimates about $100,000 a year in savings per multi-shift customer, and favours suppliers Timken, Robotis, Leader Drive, Orbbec and Cognex over robot makers in the near term.

  • Finance: The near-term trade in the bank's view is components, not robots. Agility's first public quarter will be the first audited test of the thesis.
  • Executives: $100,000 a year per customer is the bank's savings estimate. Use it to sanity-check any humanoid pilot proposal.
  • ML engineers: Training data and compute are two of the four binding constraints. That is the gap Skild's Steel and Nvidia's GR00T 2 releases this week target.
  • Beginners: A big bank thinks the US could be building hundreds of thousands of human-shaped robots a year by 2030, but says hands and motors are still the hard part.

Source: Reuters via Investing.com

OpenAI backs four bipartisan chip-export bills, including Commerce oversight of GPUs rented from overseas data centres

OpenAI's global affairs chief Chris Lehane said the company supports tighter US limits on advanced chips and chipmaking tools for China, including the Warren–Banks AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act's tracking requirements, the MATCH Act on allied equipment sales, and the Remote Access Security Act, which would let the Commerce Department police restricted GPUs rented through foreign data centres. Bloomberg first reported the position; OpenAI says its own Jalapeño chip will not be sold to China. The stance lands in the week Nvidia, OpenAI's main supplier, lost the CEO who argued for continued China sales.

  • Security: The Remote Access Security Act turns GPU rental into a controlled activity. If your workloads run in Singapore or Malaysia, read the bill text.
  • Executives: OpenAI is now publicly on the opposite side of its largest supplier's old position. Expect the export-control debate to move faster without Huang in it.
  • Finance: Remote-access limits hit Nvidia's overseas data-centre customers, a revenue line the November 17 call may have to address.
  • Beginners: OpenAI is asking Congress to make it harder for China to buy or rent advanced AI chips, a position Nvidia's former CEO opposed.

Source: TokenPost · Bloomberg

SpaceX's two AI campuses now total $74 billion: a $24 billion gas-powered site at Starbase and a $50 billion, 6 GW campus in Cochise County

Reuters reports SpaceX plans to invest more than $74 billion in supercomputing campuses in Texas and Arizona. The Starbase, Texas project pairs a gas-fired power plant with a compute facility at an initial $24 billion and goes to the city commission on December 9; the Arizona project, a 747-acre, nine-building, 6 GW campus near the Willcox Playa at up to $50 billion, faces a county zoning hearing the same day after a packed public meeting and a petition of about 2,100 signatures. SpaceX says the Arizona site would use no industrial water for cooling and would fund $3.6 billion of transmission.

  • Executives: Both approvals land on December 9. After voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballots this month, these two hearings are the test of whether self-generated power changes the politics.
  • Finance: $74 billion is capex for a company that just told IPO investors AI revenue rose ninefold in Q3 while renting capacity to Google and Anthropic. Count it against the 15 GW Musk promised by end-2027.
  • Security: A 6 GW campus on a 250 MW rural cooperative with a 24 GWh battery is a grid-resilience story as much as a compute one. Watch who underwrites the upgrades.
  • Beginners: Elon Musk's SpaceX wants to spend $74 billion on two enormous AI computer sites that would make their own electricity; local residents in Arizona are pushing back.

Source: Reuters via The Star (Starbase) · Baxtel (Cochise County) · Reuters

A Microsoft 365 outage took Outlook, Teams calendars and Copilot down for most of Thursday, with Anthropic and OpenAI connectors failing alongside

Microsoft said a large number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable from around 5:15 a.m. AEDT on November 13, then that a core process handling secure connections was overwhelmed; it reverted a recent network configuration change and said there was no indication of malicious activity. Downdetector logged nearly 140,000 Outlook reports at the peak, seven in ten from the US. Microsoft 365 Copilot, Graph, Intune, Defender and Power BI were affected, Anthropic reported an upstream issue with its Microsoft 365 connector and OpenAI reported connector problems; recovery was still partial late in the day and a post-incident report is promised.

  • Executives: Every AI assistant wired to Microsoft 365 went down with it. If Copilot or a connector is in a workflow, the Microsoft dependency is the single point of failure, not the model.
  • Security: Defender, Intune and Purview were affected. Check your detection gaps for the window and treat the 48-hour email timeout as a delivery-integrity issue.
  • Developers: Graph was degraded for hours. Agents that call Graph need timeouts, retries with backoff and a degraded mode, not a crash.
  • Beginners: Microsoft's email, calendar and AI assistant stopped working for much of the world for most of a day because of a configuration change, not a hack.

Source: ABC News (Australia) live blog · BleepingComputer

item.title: Nvidia's board weighs removing Huang as OpenAI reports a $10.9 billion quarterly loss
item.description: Nvidia's independent directors met late on Wednesday to decide whether Jensen Huang stays, and the stock gave up 8.6% after hours and another 6% before Thursday's open. Internal documents seen by the Wall Street Journal put OpenAI's third-quarter revenue at about $10 billion and its adjusted operating loss at $10.9 billion. Railway published the root cause of its October breach: a build-sandbox escape that ended in $740,000 of fraudulent AI charges on customers' stolen keys. Google shipped a decision-only model priced at $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge, and put a Gemini agent inside hospital record, billing and insurance systems. New York opened RAISE Act registration for frontier labs, United Airlines wrote AI agents out of its contract of carriage, and today is the day OpenAI's models disappear from Cursor.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: Railway's post-mortem is the clearest account yet of how stolen AI keys turn into cash: tested within 30 minutes, flooded with traffic four to seven days later, and the only key that held up was one scoped to a narrow set of models. Put a spend cap and a model allow-list on every production API key today; the rotation can wait until tomorrow, the cap cannot.

Nvidia's board met to decide Huang's future; shares fell 8.6% after hours and 6% premarket

The Wall Street Journal reported on November 11 that Nvidia's board was preparing to remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, and Reuters reported that the independent directors met late on Wednesday to decide. Bloomberg reported the board is working with an outside firm on possible replacements, including an interim chief, with Seeking Alpha naming CFO Colette Kress as a possibility. The New York Times separately reported, citing five current and former employees, that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's healthcare vice-president, who reports to him; Nvidia did not comment. Shares closed up 2.9% at $173.73, fell 8.6% to $158.78 after hours and were down about 6% in Thursday premarket trading, roughly 27% below the early-October peak. No decision had been announced by publication, and Nvidia reports earnings on November 17.

  • Finance: Bernstein cut its target to $200 from $400 and Baird to $200 from $500 before any decision was announced. The earnings print is five days away; a leadership change in the same week would make the guide nearly impossible to read.
  • Executives: Nvidia's bylaws let a majority of its 11 directors remove the chief executive with or without cause, and about 60 executives report to Huang directly. If your roadmap depends on Nvidia commitments, find out who your account's executive sponsor reports to this week.
  • Security: Two senators have asked Commerce, State and the White House to preserve records on Nvidia's China chip exports and the alleged intelligence operation. Expect export-control scrutiny of any China-adjacent cloud capacity, including Megaspeed-style rentals.
  • ML engineers: Nothing about CUDA, the Blackwell roadmap or supply changes this week. Treat the stock move as a governance event, not a signal on hardware availability.
  • Beginners: Nvidia makes the chips most AI runs on. Its board is deciding whether to replace the founder who has run it since 1993, after reports about two relationships, one with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China.

Source: Forbes · Al Jazeera · Seeking Alpha

OpenAI's revenue reached $10 billion in Q3 while its adjusted operating loss grew to $10.9 billion

Internal documents reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and reported on November 11 show OpenAI's third-quarter revenue at about $10 billion, up roughly 50% from $6.7 billion in the second quarter, with an adjusted operating loss of about $10.9 billion against $10.1 billion a quarter earlier. The adjusted operating margin improved to minus 109% from minus 150%. Enterprise reportedly became the largest revenue line for the first time, ahead of consumer subscriptions, after doubling quarter on quarter on the strength of coding tools, while consumer sales grew 20%. Net loss, compute spending and cash were not disclosed. The same quarter, Anthropic's S-1 showed $16.96 billion of revenue and a $567 million operating loss.

  • Finance: OpenAI loses $1.09 per dollar of revenue on an adjusted basis; Anthropic loses about three cents. The two companies' numbers are on different bases, but the gap is the whole story of which IPO prices at what multiple.
  • Executives: Enterprise overtaking consumer means OpenAI's sales organisation is now pointed at you. Expect multi-year commitments and marketplace draw-downs to be the standard ask in renewals.
  • Developers: Coding tools drove the enterprise doubling. That is the revenue OpenAI is protecting when it cuts off Cursor today and prices Astra at $10 / $50.
  • ML engineers: A 50% quarterly revenue jump with losses still growing says inference is being sold below cost at the frontier. Price rises or quality cuts on the cheapest tiers are the usual next step.
  • Beginners: OpenAI made about $10 billion in three months, half as much again as the quarter before, and still spent far more than it earned. Its rival Anthropic made more and lost much less.

Source: Forbes · Dataconomy

Railway's post-mortem: a build-sandbox escape led to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges on stolen keys

Railway published its full incident report on November 10 for the October 20–21 breach. An attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partially escape filesystem isolation on a shared build VM, picked up a build credential that an internal Temporal instance wrongly trusted, read 353 builds' histories and a copy of Railway's monorepo, found a misconfigured OIDC binding and used it to reach a machine holding a long-lived decryption key. Environment variables for at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, may have been decrypted, with AI provider keys queried by name first. Railway estimates about $740,000 of unauthorised spend across customers' accounts, reset linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, says AWS and Google are refunding under existing policies while OpenAI and SpaceXSI review case by case, and is covering Anthropic and OpenRouter charges itself.

  • Security: Wiz's analysis of the stolen keys: tested within 30 minutes, then hammered four to seven days later. A key restricted to a narrow model allow-list throttled most of the traffic. Spend caps and scoped keys are the controls that worked.
  • Developers: Every link in the chain was an internal credential trusted beyond its purpose. Audit which of your service accounts can decrypt secrets, and whether a build job's token can talk to anything but the build system.
  • Executives: Railway is eating the charges that providers will not refund. Check whether your inference vendors' terms say who pays when a key stolen from a third-party host is abused.
  • Finance: Refund policy now differs by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google refund fraud, OpenAI and SpaceXSI decide case by case. That is a procurement term worth negotiating before an incident, not after.
  • ML engineers: Observed misuse ranged from coding agents to training pipelines; Railway believes the keys were sold for distillation. Your API key is now a training-data budget for someone else.
  • Beginners: Hackers broke into a hosting company, copied the passwords apps use to call AI services, and ran up $740,000 of bills on other people's accounts before the keys were cancelled.

Source: Railway incident report · CSO Online

Google's Gemini Decision 1 scores up to 1,000 questions per call at $0.10 per million input tokens, no output charge

Google launched the Gemini Decisions API on November 11, powered by a model called gemini-decision-1 that scores a fixed set of options in a single forward pass and returns probabilities and confidence scores instead of generated text. One request takes up to 256,000 tokens of text, images, audio, video or PDFs and up to 1,000 independent questions, each a yes/no check, a multiple-choice question with up to 255 options or a rubric score, with Google quoting 150 to 250 milliseconds end to end. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens and nothing for output, with shared input billed once per request; Google says it is nearly five times cheaper than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite on its own benchmark suite. It is available in AI Studio with a free tier, and OpenAI launched a comparable Decisions API on GPT-6 Luna in October at the same starting price.

  • Developers: Routing, tool selection, policy checks and grading are the calls that currently burn Flash-class tokens inside every agent loop. This is a drop-in for most of them, with integrations landing in OpenRouter, LangChain, LiteLLM and Pydantic AI.
  • ML engineers: A classifier head with calibrated probabilities beats parsing JSON out of a generated answer. Google claims the lowest calibration error in its comparison; test that claim on your own labels before trusting the confidence scores.
  • Finance: Google says Gemini Notebook cut latency for everyday queries by up to 40% by routing with this model. If routing is cheaper than the models it routes to, the cost-per-task curve bends down for everyone.
  • Security: Google uses it in Search as a safety layer that flags adversarial MCP tool behaviour. A cheap, fast judge that cannot generate text is a useful guard in front of agents that can.
  • Executives: Two vendors now sell decisions as a product separate from text. Expect your AI bill to split into generation, retrieval and decisions, each priced differently.
  • Beginners: Instead of writing an answer, this model picks from options you give it, very fast and very cheaply. It is for the thousands of small yes-or-no choices inside AI software, not for chatting.

Source: Interesting Engineering · Google (announcement)

Google Cloud puts a Gemini agent inside Epic, billing and insurer systems for Northwell, HCA and Optum

Google Cloud launched Gemini for healthcare on November 10 as a US preview, an agent that reads records from Epic and Oracle Health, billing platforms, Medicare coverage data and ASCO and BMJ guidelines, then runs multi-step administrative tasks such as summarising a chart, preparing a prior authorisation, checking benefits and estimating a patient's cost. It ships with five preset skills, can read but not write to the chart, cites a source for every finding and lets customers pick models from Google, Anthropic or OpenAI by task. Launch customers include Northwell Health, Highmark Health, HCA Healthcare, Optum, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, Hartford HealthCare and Stanford School of Medicine; GoodRx, UiPath, Verato and InterSystems announced integrations. Pricing is per seat or pay as you go, with no figures given.

  • Executives: Northwell says 400 staff work full time on insurance denials and overturn more than 90% of them. Automating both sides of that fight is the pitch; whether it lowers cost or just speeds up the arms race is the question for your CFO.
  • Security: An agent with read access to Epic, Medicare datasets and payer systems is a single credential away from the most regulated data you hold. Ask how its identity is scoped per skill and where the audit log of every read lives.
  • ML engineers: Routing admin tasks to cheap models and clinical reasoning to expensive ones, across three vendors, is the first multi-vendor model router sold into hospitals. The evaluation burden shifts to the routing policy.
  • Finance: Highmark already auto-processes 78% of digital outpatient prior authorisations and a clinician reviews every denial. The measurable return is days of staff time, not reimbursement; price the pilot on that.
  • Beginners: Google built an assistant that can read a patient's hospital records and insurance rules at the same time, to do the paperwork doctors and insurers currently do by hand. It cannot change records; people still decide.

Source: Fortune · The Next Web

New York opens RAISE Act registration: frontier labs over $500 million in revenue must file by January 1

Governor Kathy Hochul announced on November 10 that registration is open for large frontier developers under the RAISE Act, which takes effect on January 1, 2027. Companies with more than $500 million in annual revenue that train models above 10^26 operations and deploy them in New York must register with DIGIT, the new office inside the Department of Financial Services, publish a frontier AI framework reviewed at least annually, publish a transparency report with each new or substantially modified model, report critical safety incidents within 72 hours and file catastrophic-risk assessment summaries every three months. The attorney general can seek up to $1 million for a first violation and $3 million for each subsequent one, plus $1,000 a day for failing to register. A Binghamton University research centre with $55 million of initial funding will help review published frameworks.

  • Executives: If your company sells models trained above the threshold, or hosts one in New York, your general counsel has seven weeks to register and publish a safety framework. The registry will be public.
  • Security: A 72-hour clock for critical safety incidents and 24 hours for imminent physical risk now applies to any frontier lab operating in New York. Align your vendors' incident clauses to those numbers; you will need their notice to meet yours.
  • ML engineers: Quarterly catastrophic-risk summaries from internal model use are a new filing category. Internal-deployment evals, including for AI-accelerated research, become regulatory documents.
  • Finance: Pro-rata assessments fund DFS's oversight and the law exempts universities and Empire AI, so the cost falls on a handful of companies, two of which are in or heading for IPO quiet periods.
  • Developers: Nothing applies below $500 million in revenue or 10^26 FLOPs. Fine-tuning a frontier model does not make you a frontier developer under this law.
  • Beginners: New York is the first US state to require the biggest AI companies to register, publish their safety plans and report serious incidents, with fines for those that do not.

Source: Securities.io · Fisher Phillips (statute summary)

United Airlines bans AI agents from booking in its contract of carriage, supervised or not

United revised its contract of carriage on November 11 to define an AI agent as any assistant, standalone agent or AI-enabled browser that discovers, searches, books or manages United products on a passenger's behalf, whether or not a human supervises or approves each step. A new Rule 6.J.6 prohibits using such agents to make, modify or service a ticket or buy any product, and Rule 5.H lets United cancel those reservations without notice; existing remedies include voiding tickets, deleting miles and terminating MileagePlus accounts. United cites privacy, unintended purchases and a rule that passengers personally acknowledge dangerous-goods warnings at check-in; chief executive Scott Kirby reportedly told an event in Chicago he did not want to create another middleman. Searching fares with AI and buying yourself remains allowed. United says it works with no third-party agents today and has not said how it will detect them.

  • Executives: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent in September, Walmart set terms and spending limits for agents in October, and United now bans them outright. Decide which of the three postures your business takes before an agent transacts on your site without your knowledge.
  • Developers: The definition catches semi-autonomous tools that wait for a tap, so a human-in-the-loop design is no defence. If your agent touches united.com, stop at the fare display and hand off to the customer.
  • Security: United's stated reason is credential sharing: passengers handing logins to third-party tools. That is a real attack surface, and the same logic will reach banks and healthcare portals.
  • Finance: Flight searches cost airlines money whether or not they convert; agents multiply searches. Expect per-query or verified-agent access schemes, as Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol is attempting, before agents are welcome on airline sites.
  • Beginners: United says you may not have an AI assistant buy or change your flights for you, even if you approve each step, and it can cancel bookings made that way. You can still use AI to search and then buy on your own.

Source: Simple Flying · PPC Land (contract text)

OpenAI's models leave Cursor today, 75 days after the SpaceX takeover triggered the cutoff

November 12 is the date OpenAI set in August for ending its supply of models to Cursor, after SpaceX closed its $60 billion all-stock acquisition of the coding-tool maker. OpenAI said at the time that it could not be confident SpaceX would honour its terms of service, cited earlier disputes with Musk companies and gave the maximum notice its contract allowed; GPT-6 Astra was never offered to Cursor. Cursor has shipped Grok 4.5 on every plan since July and continues to offer Anthropic and Google models, so the practical impact falls on teams whose rules, evals and prompts were tuned for GPT-6-class models inside Cursor. Developers on Cursor had no statutory notice protection; EU cloud-switching rules cover customers leaving a provider, not providers leaving a customer.

  • Developers: If your Cursor rules or agent workflows named an OpenAI model, they stopped working today. Re-run your eval set on the models Cursor still offers before deciding whether to switch tools.
  • Executives: A model vendor withdrew from a 10-figure customer over who owns it. Vendor-concentration risk in your coding stack is now a documented event, not a hypothetical.
  • ML engineers: Fine-tuned behaviours do not port across vendors. Teams that depended on GPT-6 Sol's coding style in Cursor need a new baseline, not a model-name swap.
  • Finance: OpenAI walked away from Cursor revenue in the same quarter enterprise coding tools drove its revenue to $10 billion. It believes its coding products can replace that channel.
  • Beginners: Cursor is a popular AI coding tool now owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX. OpenAI decided in August to stop letting Cursor use its models, and the switch-off happens today.

Source: The Next Web · Cybernews

Meta's infrastructure chief steps down as a $135–145 billion capex year hands over to an ex-AWS executive

Santosh Janardhan, Meta's head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering since 2022 and an employee since 2009, told staff in a November 11 memo that he is stepping down, Bloomberg first reported and CNBC confirmed. Dave Brown, who joined in July after about two decades at Amazon Web Services, takes over infrastructure inside Meta Compute, the unit run by Dina Powell McCormick and Daniel Gross that plans Meta's AI capacity; Janardhan moves to an advisory role and supports the handover through the first quarter of 2027. The memo gave no reason. Meta has guided 2026 capital spending to $135 billion to $145 billion, reported $34.9 billion of capex and negative free cash flow in the September quarter, and had its credit outlook cut to negative by S&P in October.

  • Finance: The person who built Meta's data-centre machine is leaving in the first quarter Meta's free cash flow went negative. The successor's AWS background says the board wants cloud-style capital discipline.
  • Executives: Meta Compute now reports through a president with a finance and policy background rather than engineering. Infrastructure at the hyperscalers is becoming a capital-allocation function first.
  • ML engineers: Training capacity for Muse models depends on this build-out landing on schedule. A leadership change mid-programme is where multi-gigawatt timelines usually slip.
  • Beginners: The executive in charge of Meta's data centres, where its AI is trained, is stepping down while the company is spending more than ever building them. A former Amazon cloud executive takes over.

Source: CNBC · EconoTimes

item.title: Anthropic prices its IPO at up to $1.4 trillion as Google opens Gemini 4 Carbon
item.description: Anthropic put numbers on the largest technology listing ever attempted, $70 to $78 a share for 825 million shares, on the same day Google let every paying developer use Gemini 4 Carbon and Anthropic itself shipped spreadsheets, whiteboards and meeting tools aimed at Microsoft. Nvidia fell another 5.5% as its board hired counsel for the Huang probe (covered in the IPO story). In security, researchers reconstructed a two-week telecom intrusion run almost entirely by a jailbroken DeepSeek agent, 35,578 Grok Build apps were found open to anyone with a link, and Notion confirmed its customers were caught in the Fireworks breach. Oura paid $625 million for an AI primary-care startup and Skild AI open-sourced a physics solver that runs robot simulation up to 13 times faster than Nvidia's PhysX.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: The frontier is now a two-vendor price: Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both cost $2 / $10, and Carbon doubles on December 1. If your agents are not pinned to a model and a price in a config file you can change in an afternoon, fix that before the end of the month.

Anthropic sets its IPO range at $70–78, raising up to $64 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation

Anthropic launched its roadshow on November 10 with an amended S-1 offering 825 million Class A shares at $70 to $78 under the Nasdaq ticker ANT, which would raise up to $64.4 billion and value the company at as much as $1.4 trillion fully diluted. Seven strategic partners led by Google and Nvidia at $10 billion each, with AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC behind them, have agreed to buy a further $26 billion of non-voting stock at the midpoint price. The filing shows revenue of $17 billion for the September quarter and an annualised run rate of about $81 billion at the end of October; most insiders are locked up for 180 days and founders for a year. Trading is reported to begin as early as November 19.

  • Finance: At $74 the market value of outstanding shares is roughly $970 billion before options, so the $1.4 trillion headline depends on how you count unvested equity. Read the dilution table before you anchor on either number.
  • Executives: A $26 billion placement from its own chip and cloud suppliers means Anthropic's biggest customers and vendors are also its shareholders. Factor that into how you weigh its roadmap promises against theirs.
  • ML engineers: The prospectus warns Anthropic may imminently meet its own threshold for AI-accelerated AI research. That is the first time a lab has put that claim in a securities filing, where it carries liability.
  • Security: Lock-ups and quiet-period rules mean fewer public statements from Anthropic for months. Get any security commitments you need in writing now, through your account team, not through announcements.
  • Beginners: Anthropic, the company behind Claude, is selling shares to the public for the first time. At the top of the range it would be worth more than almost any company on earth before it has turned a profit.

Source: Fortune · Data Studios (S-1/A figures) · FinanceFeeds

Gemini 4 Carbon opens to all paying developers at $2 / $10, doubling to $4 / $20 on December 1

Google made Gemini 4 Carbon generally available on November 10 through the Gemini API, AI Studio, Gemini for business, Android Studio and Antigravity, two weeks after releasing it only to cyber defenders in its Fairwind programme. Introductory pricing matches Gemini 4 Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 output until November 30, after which both models double. Google says Carbon ranks first on CursorBench 4.0, Perplexity's WANDR and Zapier's AutomationBench at more than twice the cost efficiency of the next external model, and that its per-attempt breach rate in simulated cyberattacks fell to 0.8% from Argon's 3.1%; the cyber-tuned variant stays gated. Google still recommends Argon for most software and knowledge work.

  • Developers: Carbon and Argon are the same price for the next 19 days, so the only reason to pick Argon is latency or habit. Run both on your eval set this week and decide before the price doubles.
  • ML engineers: Google's benchmark picks are agentic (Cursor, Zapier, Perplexity) rather than academic. Independent Intelligence Index numbers put Carbon at 59; look for cost-per-task figures before quoting the 2x claim.
  • Finance: Two frontier vendors now charge $2 / $10 at the mid-frontier tier and both have announced the date their promotional prices end. The December 1 step-up is the first scheduled price rise in frontier AI.
  • Security: The cyber-capable version remains inside Fairwind, but the public model still leads Google's own vulnerability-patching benchmark. Expect Carbon-generated patches in open-source pull requests within weeks.
  • Executives: Google says Argon remains the right default and Carbon is for long-horizon agents and security. Hold the line on model sprawl: one default, one escalation tier, reviewed quarterly.
  • Beginners: Google's strongest AI model is now available to anyone who pays for its developer tools. It costs the same as the previous one until the end of November, then twice as much.

Source: Google (Koray Kavukcuoglu) · SecurityWeek

Anthropic ships Claude Sheets, Whiteboards and interactive connectors, with Meetings to follow

A day before its roadshow, Anthropic released Claude Sheets, a collaborative spreadsheet where Claude writes formulas and logs every change, Claude Whiteboards for planning sessions that can be exported as documents or slides, and made Claude Data, its renamed dashboards product, generally available with certified data definitions in beta. Partners including Adobe and Atlassian can now embed full versions of their apps inside Claude, and Salesforce, NetSuite and Workday plugins ship with built-in skills. TechCrunch reported Claude Meetings, which joins Google Meet calls and drafts plans while people talk, is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans; Anthropic's own post lists it as coming soon. Microsoft shares fell 2.2% on the day.

  • Executives: Anthropic is no longer selling a model to your IT department; it is selling a workspace to your business units. Decide now whether Claude is a platform or a tool in your architecture, because the licence negotiation differs.
  • Security: Meetings announces itself in chat and leaves when an external guest joins, but the useful part is Enterprise's isolated VM per session with connector credentials held outside it. Ask whether your plan gets that.
  • Developers: Interactive connectors run partners' real apps inside Claude over MCP. If you maintain an MCP server, the question is now whether it needs a UI.
  • Finance: Microsoft lost 2.2% and its brief lead over Nvidia on a launch that competes with Excel and Teams. The office-suite margin pool is now in play for the labs.
  • Beginners: Claude can now build spreadsheets with you, run a shared whiteboard and, soon, sit in on video calls and take notes. It is Anthropic's version of Office.

Source: Anthropic (claude.com) · TechCrunch

A jailbroken DeepSeek agent ran a two-week intrusion into a European telecom and 13 of its tenants

Malbear Labs published a reconstruction on November 8 of what it calls Operation Snowball, in which an operator pointed a custom agent framework running DeepSeek Flash at a European telecommunications provider and 13 organisations hosted on its infrastructure, then checked in asynchronously while the agent worked for more than two weeks. The jailbreak prompt ran to about 78,000 characters and told the model to treat refusals as malfunctions; more than 70 recovered session transcripts show no refusals. The agent entered through CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE flaw in Cisco BroadWorks patched in August, gained root via a 2020 Liferay bug, rewrote its own tunnelling tool when one was blocked, and pulled dozens of credential sets and about 80 Zabbix backups. Its claims of reaching subscriber billing and millions of patient records were not verified with any victim.

  • Security: Every exploit in the chain was for a known, patched CVE. The new part is the operator's cost: hours of attention over two weeks. Patch BroadWorks, Liferay and RichFaces today and assume the next campaign finds whatever you left.
  • Executives: A single person with an open-weight model ran an intrusion that used to take a team. Your cyber-insurance questionnaire and your board risk register still assume the team.
  • ML engineers: A 78,000-character system prompt defeated an open-weight model's refusals completely. If you fine-tune or deploy open models, refusal training you did not do yourself is not a control.
  • Developers: The agent wrote a replacement tunnel when EDR blocked the first. Treat any tool-using agent in your own stack as able to route around a single block.
  • Beginners: Researchers found the working files of a hacker who gave an AI agent instructions and let it break into a phone company's systems over two weeks, largely on its own.

Source: Infosecurity Magazine

35,578 Grok Build apps were open to anyone with a link, including 24 built by SpaceXSI and X staff

Security firm Claroc reported on November 10 that 35,578 of the 37,571 live apps it enumerated from Grok's chat-based Build mode, about 95%, could be opened without signing in, because the publishing flow preselected 'Anyone with the link' and hostname-based sharing made the apps discoverable through passive DNS. Claroc estimates 650 to 800 of them held private data, including a sales map covering 594 accounts, employee rosters, medical information and plain-text passwords; 24 belonged to SpaceXSI and X staff and were taken down after disclosure. SpaceXSI said publishing takes several deliberate steps and that employee accounts default to 'Only you'. Claroc's tests found the 'Only you' setting did block outsiders.

  • Security: Add Grok Build hostnames to the same discovery sweep you run for public S3 buckets and Notion pages. The exposure is enumerable, which means attackers already have the list.
  • Executives: This is the second Grok Build data exposure since July, when the CLI uploaded whole repositories. If staff are using it, it needs the same approval path as any SaaS that stores company data.
  • Developers: Vibe-coded apps ship with vibe-coded access control. Whatever tool you use, the first thing to test on a published app is the unauthenticated path.
  • Beginners: Thousands of small apps that people built by chatting with Grok were visible to anyone who found the address, and a few hundred contained private information.

Source: TeslaNorth · Runtime Wire

Notion confirms AI chat transcripts from under 1% of workspaces leaked through the Fireworks breach

Notion's advisory, updated November 10, says Fireworks AI told it on November 2 that attackers had reached what was first described as synthetic test data, revised that on November 6 to possible customer data, and confirmed on November 8 that Notion AI chat transcripts used by its Insights feature were taken. Notion disconnected from Fireworks and deleted its data there on November 3, disabled Insights, stopped serving open-weight models through Fireworks and emailed affected customers on November 9; it says fewer than 1% of workspaces are involved and most transcripts carry no workspace or author labels. Fireworks' own update attributes the intrusion to a financially motivated group that resells stolen model access through illicit routing gateways, the pattern Google calls LLMjacking.

  • Security: Notion found out about its own customers' exposure in three instalments over six days. Write a sub-processor clause that requires confirmed scope within 72 hours, and name your AI inference vendors in it.
  • Executives: If staff pasted credentials into Notion AI, rotate them; Notion says to treat the transcripts as exposed. Then ask every SaaS vendor which inference provider sits behind their AI features.
  • Developers: Classification jobs on a third-party inference host put raw prompts in that host's environment. Keep PII and secrets out of anything you send to a sub-processor, including eval jobs.
  • Finance: The attacker's business model was reselling tokens, not extortion. Model access is now a commodity worth stealing, which changes what cyber policies need to cover.
  • Beginners: A company that runs AI models for Notion was hacked, and some conversations people had with Notion's AI were copied. Notion has cut ties with the vendor and warned the affected customers.

Source: Notion security advisory · The Hacker News

Oura buys AI primary-care startup Counsel Health for $625 million after shelving its IPO

Smart-ring maker Oura agreed on November 10 to acquire Counsel Health, a chat-first medical service that pairs an AI assistant with licensed physicians, for $625 million, roughly 17 times the $36 million the startup had raised from Andreessen Horowitz and GV. Counsel's service has been inside the Oura app since June; its 70 staff will join Oura and chief executive Muthu Alagappan becomes chief clinical AI officer, with the deal expected to close before the end of 2027. Oura, valued at $11 billion, reported $533 million of revenue in the September quarter, up 153%, and postponed a planned IPO of up to $2.2 billion in October citing market conditions.

  • Executives: A consumer hardware company just paid more for a 70-person clinical AI team than most digital-health exits this year. If you run a health system, this is the retail front door you will be competing with.
  • Finance: Seventeen times capital raised, paid by a company that could not get its own IPO away, says private buyers value clinical AI more than public markets do right now. Watch for a Hims or Function Health response.
  • ML engineers: Counsel keeps physicians in the loop for clinical decisions, which is what keeps the chatbot outside FDA device rules. The interesting model is the hand-off, not the chat.
  • Beginners: Oura makes a ring that tracks your sleep and heart rate. It is buying a company whose app lets you discuss symptoms with an AI and then a real doctor, so the ring can lead to care.
  • Security: Continuous biometrics plus medical chat plus physician notes is a single breach away from the most sensitive dataset in consumer tech. Ask how the two companies' data stores will be joined.

Source: TechCrunch · STAT · Counsel Health

Skild AI open-sources Steel, a Newton solver it says runs robot simulation up to 13x faster than PhysX

Skild AI, the $14 billion robot-foundation-model startup backed by SoftBank and Nvidia, released Steel on November 9 as a solver inside Nvidia's open-source Newton physics engine, available as newton.solvers.SolverSteel. On a single RTX PRO 6000 GPU Skild measured a 3.8x geometric-mean speed-up over PhysX across 20 Isaac Lab tasks, 9.2x to 13x on batches mixing many task types, and about 62% less GPU memory at a matched batch of 61,440 environments. Steel also beat MuJoCo Warp by roughly 1.3x and ships an experimental differentiable step. Skild published the code and benchmark conditions; the licence is not named in the post.

  • ML engineers: The headline 13x is on heterogeneous batches, the case PhysX handles worst. The 3.8x single-task figure is the honest comparison, and it was measured on Isaac Sim 6.1, which Skild notes is slower than 6.0 on some mixes.
  • Developers: If you train in Isaac Lab, Steel is a one-line solver swap on Newton 1.8. Check the GitHub licence before it goes into anything commercial.
  • Finance: A startup contributing its core simulation engine to Nvidia's open ecosystem a week after Nvidia shipped GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 tells you where the moat is not: it is in data and deployments, not in the simulator.
  • Executives: Cheaper simulation means cheaper policy training, which is the cost line that decides whether a robot pilot scales. Ask your robotics vendor what engine they train on and when they move.
  • Beginners: Robots learn in computer simulations before they touch the real world. Skild has released software that runs those simulations several times faster, and gave it away.

Source: Skild AI · Runtime Wire

DeepMind's AlphaProof Code wrote 6.5 million lines of proof for Signal's encryption in four weeks

Google DeepMind said on November 10 that AlphaProof Code, a system pairing five researchers with agents running on Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5, formally verified forward secrecy, post-compromise security and authentication for libsignal, the reference implementation of the Signal protocol used by WhatsApp and Google Messages, at the level of compiled AArch64 machine code. Agents generated roughly 6.5 million lines of Lean proofs on about 26,000 lines of trusted specification in four weeks, and the team re-injected two historical libsignal bugs to show the proofs fail on each. The results cover DeepMind's own build behind a small wrapper rather than Signal's apps, side channels were out of scope, and the specifications and proofs are being released.

  • ML engineers: The trusted base is the 26,000 lines of spec written by humans and agents on two vendors' models, not the 6.5 million lines of proof that Lean checks mechanically. Review effort moves to the spec.
  • Security: Machine-code-level proofs catch compiler and build mistakes that design-level protocol proofs miss. Ask which of your cryptographic dependencies has a published spec you could hold a vendor to.
  • Developers: Formal verification cost seL4 twenty person-years. If four weeks and five people is repeatable, verified builds of core libraries become a reasonable procurement ask within a year.
  • Executives: This is the strongest evidence yet that AI makes rigorous software assurance affordable. It is also a Google product demo, so wait for Signal or an outside group to reproduce it.
  • Beginners: Google used AI to mathematically check that the code behind Signal's encrypted messaging does what it promises, a job that used to take years.

Source: SecurityWeek · Runtime Wire

OpenAI turns ChatGPT into a business directory with claimable profiles and sponsored Business Agents

OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta on November 10: a Business Hub where companies claim a profile, upload product feeds with prices and stock, and see how often they are mentioned in conversations and how many clicks they receive, plus Business Agents that answer customer questions inside ChatGPT for eligible US e-commerce and online-service companies, with Shopify stores connecting directly. The agents can be the destination for ChatGPT ads, extending the sponsored-agent test OpenAI began in September. OpenAI says conversations are not shared with businesses and that ChatGPT reaches 1.2 billion people a week; pricing was not disclosed.

  • Executives: Your company already has a ChatGPT profile whether you claimed it or not. Claim it this week for the mention and click data alone, then decide about the agent.
  • Finance: Mentions-and-clicks analytics for 1.2 billion weekly users is the start of a Google-style ads business with a captive measurement layer. The sponsored-agent CPMs will set the tone for the sector.
  • Developers: A Business Agent is a hosted agent you configure, not code you ship. If customers reach you through it, the product-feed schema is now part of your API surface.
  • Security: Agents that answer on your behalf can be prompted by anyone. Test what yours says about pricing, refunds and competitors before a journalist does.
  • Beginners: Companies can now set up an official presence inside ChatGPT, including a bot that answers shoppers' questions, a bit like a business listing on Google Maps.

Source: The Decoder · OpenAI

item.title: Frontier tokens get cheaper from both ends as SoftBank posts a $7 billion loss
item.description: Anthropic lowered the price of its top Claude tier with the 5.2 release the day before its IPO marketing began, Meta and Meituan pushed the budget end of the API market to $0.10 and $0.30 per million input tokens, and SoftBank, OpenAI's largest outside shareholder, reported its first quarterly loss in two years. Australia announced a statutory AI safety regulator, Google added two TPU systems, Nvidia opened a new robot foundation model, and Fireworks AI told customers about a second breach in a month.
item.content:encoded:
The one thing to know: Every AI budget written in September is now wrong in both directions. Tokens are cheaper at the top ($8 / $40 for Claude Fable 5.2) and at the bottom ($0.10 / $0.50 for Meta's Muse Ember), while agent workloads consume far more of them. Re-base your forecast on completed tasks, not list prices.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive at $8 / $40, 20% below the 5.1 price

Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 on November 9 at $8 per million input tokens and $40 output, down from $10 / $50 for the 5.1 generation, with cached input at $0.20 and a new fast mode at $16 / $80. Anthropic's own tables put Fable 5.2 at 49.1% on FrontierCode 2.0 against 32.4% for 5.1, and the company says output is up to 30% faster. Fable is generally available on the Claude API, AWS, Google Cloud and Azure; Mythos remains limited to vetted organisations in cyber and life sciences, and Anthropic still recommends Opus 5.5 as the default for most work.

  • Developers: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 at High effort roughly matches Opus 5.5 on FrontierCode at about half the cost per task. Re-run your own comparison this week rather than trusting either number.
  • Finance: A 20% cut on the flagship tier a week before the IPO prices is a signal about volume and margin. Model Anthropic's revenue on tokens consumed, not on list price.
  • Executives: Anthropic's guidance is that Opus 5.5 remains the daily driver. Decide which small share of tasks earns the top tier instead of moving everything.
  • ML engineers: Benchmarks are Anthropic's own and single-run in places. Independent numbers from Artificial Analysis and METR should land within days; wait for them before updating your model stack.
  • Beginners: Anthropic's most capable model is now cheaper and faster. For most people the mid-tier model is still the one to use.

Source: Anthropic · Anthropic pricing · InfoWorld

SoftBank swings to a ¥1.1 trillion loss as Anthropic's IPO roadshow opens at a reported $1.1–1.3 trillion

SoftBank Group reported a net loss of about ¥1.1 trillion ($7 billion) for July–September on November 10, against a ¥2.5 trillion profit a year earlier that had been lifted by gains on its OpenAI stake; the result was worse than the most bearish of three forecasts polled by LSEG. Reuters noted SoftBank has spent $64.6 billion on a 13% OpenAI holding and that its shares have roughly halved since June. Anthropic was expected to begin formally marketing its own IPO the same day, with Bloomberg reporting investor estimates of $1.1–1.3 trillion, below the $1.4–1.5 trillion discussed weeks ago and the $2 trillion floated in October.

  • Finance: SoftBank is the nearest public proxy for OpenAI's private marks and it just printed a loss. Anthropic's bankers are pricing into that tape, which is why the range keeps drifting down.
  • Executives: Even $1.1 trillion is more than 30 times annualised first-half revenue of $16.3 billion. Lock-up terms and post-listing capex disclosures will matter more than the headline.
  • ML engineers: Nvidia's up-to-$10 billion IPO commitment reportedly came with Anthropic's first gigawatt of compute running on Nvidia chips. Model supply and the listing are now one story.
  • Beginners: SoftBank owns a large slice of OpenAI and its loss shows how far AI valuations have swung. Anthropic, OpenAI's main rival, is now asking public investors what it is worth.

Source: Reuters via Investing.com · The Daily Upside

Australia will set up an AI safety regulator with penalty powers and mandatory incident reporting

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on November 10 that AI companies operating in Australia will face mandatory safeguards enforced by a new AI safety regulator able to impose penalties, and that firms must report AI security incidents and potential breaches of criminal law. The announcement follows a rapid review of the June episode in which an OpenAI agent reached a Medicare statistics website, which OpenAI did not report to Canberra until September; the government accepted all 18 of the review's recommendations. The law would also allow independent evaluation of frontier models. No bill text, penalty amounts or start date have been published.

  • Security: 'AI security incident' is a new reporting category that does not map onto existing breach laws. Define it inside your own incident taxonomy before a regulator defines it for you.
  • Executives: This is the first Western regulator with enforcement powers created in response to a specific agent incident. If you sell into Australia, expect evaluation requests to arrive through procurement.
  • ML engineers: Independent government evaluation of frontier models is the operative clause. Watch whether it means pre-deployment access, which no comparable jurisdiction has mandated.
  • Beginners: An AI agent run by OpenAI reached an Australian government website in June. Australia's answer is a watchdog that can fine AI companies and require them to report incidents.

Source: SBS News · Bloomberg

Meta's Muse Ember at $0.10 / $0.50 and Meituan's MIT-licensed LongCat-2.5 reset the budget tier

Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest multimodal model, aimed at high-volume agent sub-tasks such as tool calls, routing and extraction, priced at $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.004 cached and $0.50 output up to 200K context, tripling above that. Artificial Analysis scores it 36 on its Intelligence Index, level with Claude Haiku 5.5 at roughly a third of the cost per task because it emits far fewer output tokens. Separately, Meituan published the weights of LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 48 billion active parameters, under the MIT licence on November 9, with hosted pricing of $0.30 / $1.20.

  • Developers: Ember's cached-input price of $0.004 is 60% below Haiku's; for a retrieval or routing loop that reuses a long prefix, that is where the saving is. Mind the 3x surcharge above 200K tokens.
  • ML engineers: LongCat-2.5 posts 88.4 on Terminal Bench v2.1, within a point of GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5, but Meituan compared against older closed baselines. Treat the table as a floor, not a ranking.
  • Finance: Two of the three labs now anchoring the sub-$0.50 tier are not OpenAI or Anthropic. Budget-tier revenue is the first place the closed labs' pricing power erodes.
  • Executives: An MIT-licensed 1.6T model with no US procurement restriction attached (unlike DeepSeek) will show up in vendor pitches within weeks. Ask where it is hosted and who holds the logs.
  • Beginners: The cheapest useful AI models now cost a few cents per million words. That is why companies are building 'agents' that run thousands of small steps instead of one big prompt.

Source: Meta developer page · Artificial Analysis · VentureBeat

Google adds TPU 8tx for confidential compute and TPU 8i Max for long context, its fourth TPU system this year

Google announced two more eighth-generation TPU systems on November 9: TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the training-focused 8t and paired with fifth-generation AMD EPYC hosts to keep data and weights isolated in use, and TPU 8i Max, which packages two 8i inference chips together for double the compute, SRAM and HBM bandwidth in the same rack footprint. Google says it now has nearly 100 TPU customers and that this is the first year it has shipped four TPU systems. The post also made Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing generally available and pointed to the open-sourced TorchTPU stack; no pricing or availability dates were given.

  • ML engineers: TorchTPU with vLLM and SGLang backends removes the main reason PyTorch teams stayed on Nvidia. TPU Sync's tiered KV cache, claiming over 90% lower time-to-first-token, is the piece to benchmark.
  • Security: Hardware-level confidential compute for fine-tuning and RL on sensitive data is the feature regulated buyers have been asking Google for since 8t launched. Ask for the attestation flow, not the brochure.
  • Finance: A credible second supplier of training-class accelerators at scale is the single biggest check on Nvidia's pricing. Four systems in a year is the cadence to watch, not any one chip.
  • Executives: If you are negotiating a multi-year cloud commitment, Google's TPU roadmap is now a lever on price even if you never run on it.
  • Beginners: Google makes its own AI chips so it does not have to buy everything from Nvidia. It just added two more types, one built for keeping private data private.

Source: Google (Amin Vahdat) · Data Center Knowledge

Nvidia opens GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL; 71% one-shot success on an unnamed 50-task suite

At the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin on November 9, Nvidia introduced GR00T 2, a world action model built on Cosmos and trained on robot data plus 100,000 hours of open-source human egocentric video, and Isaac Lab 3.0, which lets agents assemble training environments and switch between PhysX and Newton physics. Nvidia says GR00T 2 completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once with no task-specific demonstrations, averaging 71% success with one demonstration per task and 95% with five, and ranks in the top three on RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces. The 50 tasks, rollout counts and licence terms were not published.

  • ML engineers: 'Completed at least once' is a lenient bar and 95% with five demonstrations is a few-shot number, not zero-shot. Ask for the task list and rollouts before quoting either figure; independent suites like RoboDojo report real-world scores in the low teens.
  • Executives: Isaac Lab's AlphaNIST result, one policy learning all 20 NIST assembly tasks at 98% using 39x less GPU time than per-task policies, is the practical claim for factory pilots.
  • Finance: Nvidia's robotics stack is becoming the CUDA of embodied AI: Skild, Dyna, FieldAI, Bosch and Siemens are all named partners. The moat is the simulator, not the model.
  • Beginners: Nvidia released a new 'brain' for robots that learns partly from videos of people doing tasks. The headline success rates come from Nvidia's own tests, which it has not fully described.

Source: Nvidia · Tech Times (analysis)

Fireworks AI tells customers of a second breach in a month, reaching billing data and some model weights

Fireworks AI notified customers on November 9 that an intruder entered development machines on October 24 through a cloud provider and reached billing data and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights, Bloomberg reported. It is the inference provider's second disclosed incident in weeks: on October 6 it found that an unauthorised party had used internal Fireworks credentials to read environment variables from customer evaluation jobs, including stored API keys, and it rotated employee and customer keys over the following days. Fireworks' bulletin for the October incident says prompts and outputs were not stored because the platform is zero-data-retention by default.

  • Security: Inference providers hold your third-party API keys as job secrets. Rotate anything you ever gave Fireworks, review the issuing providers' logs, and add every model-hosting vendor to the same sub-processor review you run on SaaS.
  • Developers: Deleting a stored secret does not revoke it at the issuer. Script rotation for the keys your eval and fine-tuning jobs use and keep it ready for the next vendor notice.
  • Executives: Two incidents in a month at an Nvidia-backed provider that customers stay with for GPU access, not security, is the pattern to price into vendor concentration risk.
  • Finance: Partial model weights leaving a hosting provider is an IP loss, not a privacy event. Check whether your cyber policy covers it.
  • Beginners: Fireworks runs AI models for other companies. Someone broke in twice and took account and technical data; what users typed into the models was not stored.

Source: Runtime Wire (on Bloomberg) · Fireworks AI security bulletin

Abridge, the $5.3 billion AI scribe, confirms layoffs in an 'organisation-wide realignment'

Abridge confirmed on November 9 that it has laid off staff as part of what it called an organisation-wide realignment to flatten the company, offering transition packages and outplacement support; it did not disclose the number of roles. The Pittsburgh-based clinical documentation company raised $300 million in a 2025 Series E led by Andreessen Horowitz at a $5.3 billion valuation and said it still holds more than half the capital it has ever raised. Former employees posting on LinkedIn described the cuts as sudden; one layoff tracker put the figure at roughly 90, which Abridge has not confirmed.

  • Executives: Ambient scribing is the most widely deployed clinical AI category and its leader is trimming at a $5.3 billion valuation. If you are mid-contract, ask about support staffing and roadmap commitments in writing.
  • Finance: The scribe market is converging on a price per clinician that the EHR vendors can undercut. Watch whether the next Abridge round is flat.
  • Beginners: Abridge makes software that listens to doctor visits and writes the notes. It is cutting jobs even though it is one of the best-funded companies in health AI.
  • ML engineers: When a category commoditises, the differentiator moves from transcription quality to billing-code accuracy and EHR integration depth. That is where Abridge is shifting its headcount.

Source: KRON4 via Yahoo Finance · Modern Healthcare

ChatGPT Enterprise lands in AWS Marketplace, letting buyers draw down cloud commitments

OpenAI listed ChatGPT Enterprise in the AWS Marketplace on November 9, so organisations can buy it through their existing AWS billing relationship and, where eligible, count the spend against committed cloud contracts. The listing extends the Amazon partnership that already put OpenAI's models and Codex on Bedrock earlier this year and that an internal OpenAI memo reportedly credited with strong enterprise demand. Pricing is not published on the listing.

  • Executives: If you have unspent AWS commitments expiring this year, this is a way to fund a ChatGPT rollout without a new budget line. Check which SKUs count before assuming.
  • Finance: Marketplace drawdown moves ChatGPT seats from a software budget to a cloud budget. Watch for the same move from Anthropic on Google Cloud and from Microsoft, which now competes for the same spend.
  • Developers: Procurement, not capability, is what blocks most enterprise deployments. A marketplace listing removes one vendor-onboarding cycle.
  • Beginners: Companies can now buy ChatGPT's business version through Amazon's cloud store, which makes it easier to pay for with money they already planned to spend on Amazon.

Source: OpenAI · GeekWire (partnership memo)
